Bigeye scad Selar crumenophthalmus is a commercially important carangid distributed widely across tropical and subtropical waters. Field-based studies have documented that individuals attain an ultimate total length of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], a size that reflects this species' position as a moderately large member of the scad complex. Length-frequency analyses from multiple localities indicate that puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal development, occurs when fish reach a total length of approximately 17.7 centimeters [Lp = approximately 17.7 centimeters]. This size at maturation is comparatively small relative to the asymptotic length, suggesting that energetic investment in reproduction begins relatively early in the life cycle. The reproductive strategy of this species is characterized by high fecundity and batch spawning, with females producing a large number of small pelagic eggs over an extended spawning season.

Under a consistent thermal regime of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], the daily reproductive output of this species reaches a maximum of approximately 718 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 718 eggs per day], a rate that underscores the high reproductive potential typical of many tropical carangids. This elevated fecundity is sustained over multiple spawning events throughout the breeding season and is closely tied to the warm, stable temperatures that prevail in its core habitat. The relationship between temperature and reproductive output is particularly important in Selar crumenophthalmus, as deviations from this optimal thermal condition can markedly reduce spawning frequency and egg viability. Such temperature dependence has implications for population resilience under warming sea surface scenarios.

The early life stages of Selar crumenophthalmus are brief and energetically constrained. At a water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], the interval between fertilization and hatching spans only 2.7 days [ab = 2.7 days], a rapid developmental pace consistent with the small pelagic egg size typical of this genus. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge with a dry weight of 0.000212 grams [Wwb = 0.000212 grams], reflecting the modest yolk reserves packaged within each fertilized ovum. This extremely low birth mass places a premium on the efficiency of yolk utilization during the endotrophic larval phase. The high surface-area-to-volume ratio of these tiny larvae facilitates rapid gas exchange but also renders them vulnerable to thermal and osmotic stress during the critical period before first feeding.

As individuals progress through the juvenile and adult stages, body mass increases by several orders of magnitude. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown individuals has been estimated at 4.25 kilograms [Wwi = 4.25 kilograms], a value derived from length-weight relationships calibrated for the species. This substantial increase in somatic mass reflects a growth trajectory that channels a large proportion of ingested energy into structural tissue rather than storage, a pattern common among fast-growing tropical pelagic fishes. The transformation from a planktonic larva weighing less than a milligram to a kilogram-sized adult involves a dramatic allometric shift in body plan, including the development of robust caudal musculature and the ossification of fin rays necessary for sustained swimming performance.

Longevity data for Selar crumenophthalmus, collected from otolith-based age estimates at a reference temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], indicate that the maximum recorded lifespan reaches 5 years [am = 5 years]. This relatively short life span is characteristic of a fast-living, early-maturing species that experiences high natural mortality in the pelagic environment. The trade-off between rapid maturation and extended longevity is clearly evident in this species: reproductive output is concentrated in a narrow window of adult life, with individuals typically spawning repeatedly over two to three seasons. Annual mortality rates inferred from catch curves suggest that very few individuals survive beyond their fourth year, reinforcing the selective advantage of early and copious reproduction under the warm, productive conditions that define its ecological niche.
